title: Inter-Process Communication: Component Object Model
summary: The Component Object Model (COM) is the native Windows mechanism that lets software components call each other through defined interfaces, without the caller knowing how the server is implemented. Objects are registered with a class identifier (CLSID) and created through activation calls, and the server behind an interface may be a Dynamic Link Library (DLL) loaded into the caller, an executable started as a separate process, or a service. That design makes COM useful as a local execution primitive: a script or a proxy can request a registered object, and the code behind it runs with the caller's permissions, sometimes from a binary that security tools consider trusted. Certain objects also perform other useful actions directly, such as creating scheduled tasks or writing files. Detection uses registry and object telemetry plus process creation: activation of class identifiers that a host process never normally uses, unusual server processes starting with an unfamiliar parent, and DLLs loaded from user writable paths. Legitimate software activates COM constantly, so baselines of which process creates which class carry most of the value.

beginner.definition: The Component Object Model, or COM, is a Windows way for programs to use each other's features. A program asks for an object by a registration number, and Windows starts the code behind it. Because the request is normal Windows behaviour, the work can look like a trusted program doing its job. This sub-technique differs from the parent: here the shared channel is COM itself, not pipes or another local mechanism.
beginner.whyItMatters: COM is everywhere in Windows, so simply blocking it is not an option. Attackers use it to run code while hiding behind a trusted program name. Some objects even create scheduled tasks or write files for the attacker. This can bypass tools that only look at which program was started. If you do not know which programs normally use COM on your systems, the abuse stays invisible.
howItWorks: A Windows program needs a feature that another software component already provides.
It asks for that component using a registration number called a class identifier, or CLSID.
Windows then loads the code behind it, either inside the caller or as a new process.
An attacker can make the same request and have their chosen component run.
Some components also perform useful actions for an attacker, such as creating a scheduled task.
Security tools see a trusted host making a normal call, and often allow it.
beginner.example: Imagine a workshop where any worker may borrow a power tool by writing the tool number on a form. The store room checks the number and hands the tool over. A visitor writes the number of a heavy drill on the form. The store room gives them the drill without asking why. The workshop log shows a tool borrowed by a number that looks normal. Only by comparing the forms with who usually borrows what can the manager find the odd request.
takeaways: Know which programs on your systems should use COM objects, and when.
Alert on unusual parent processes starting local COM servers.
Watch for libraries loaded from folders where ordinary users can write files.

objectives: Explain how a class identifier and an activation call create a COM object on Windows.
Describe the difference between an in-process, a local and a remote COM server.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the Dynamic Data Exchange sub-technique.
Identify the registry, process and module load evidence that reveals COM abuse.
Explain why a trusted host process can be the parent of malicious execution.
